questions.prompt: The graph below is f. What value belongs on the graph of f′ at x=1?
questions.explanation: The point x=1 lies inside the flat segment from (0,3) to (2,3). Its rise is zero over a nonzero run, so f′(1)=0. A derivative graph records slopes of f rather than copying its heights. A: The original graph is horizontal near x=1, so its local slope is zero. B: This is the original function height, not the derivative. C: This is the slope of a different segment after x=2. D: This is the slope of the original graph before x=0.

questions.prompt: The graph below is f′ for a differentiable function. At which displayed interior input does f have a local maximum?
questions.explanation: To identify a maximum of f from f′, locate a positive-to-negative sign crossing. The graph crosses that way at x=1 only. The crossings at −1 and 3 have the opposite direction and correspond to minima of f. A: That crossing is negative to positive and gives a local minimum. B: The derivative crosses from positive to negative there. C: That crossing also gives a local minimum. D: The derivative has a positive peak there, so f is still increasing through it.

questions.prompt: Which description fits the graph of f′ when f(x)=(x−2)²+3?
options: An upward parabola with vertex (2,3).
A line with slope 2 crossing the horizontal axis at x=−2.
A line with slope 2 crossing the horizontal axis at x=2.
A horizontal line at height 3.
questions.explanation: Differentiating gives f′(x)=2(x−2)=2x−4. Its graph is a straight line of slope 2 with zero at 2 and vertical intercept −4. The original parabola’s vertex height 3 disappears under differentiation. A: This describes the original function, not its derivative. B: This uses the wrong sign for the horizontal shift. C: The derivative is 2x−4, independent of the vertical shift 3. D: The original vertical shift does not become a derivative height.

questions.prompt: On an interval, the graph of f′ is below the horizontal axis but rises as x increases. Which shape should a sketch of f show there?
options: Increasing and concave up.
Decreasing and concave down.
Increasing and concave down.
Decreasing and concave up.
questions.explanation: Use two separate features of the derivative graph. Its negative heights imply f′<0, so f decreases. Its rising trend means the slopes of f become less negative, so f is concave up. Function direction and bending are independent. A: The sign of f′ is negative, so f cannot be increasing there. B: A rising derivative graph indicates positive rather than negative curvature. C: Both sign-to-feature translations are reversed. D: Negative derivative means decreasing f, while increasing derivative means concave up.

questions.prompt: The graph below is f. How should a sketch of f′ behave at x=0?
options: It should have no defined value there because the one-sided slopes of f differ.
It should have value 0 because the original graph reaches height 0.
It should have value −1 because the left segment comes first.
It should have value 1 because the right segment rises.
questions.explanation: The continuous V has a corner at 0. Its left-hand difference quotient tends to −1 and its right-hand quotient to +1. Since the limits disagree, f′(0) is undefined. A derivative sketch must not connect the two branches by inventing a value at that input. A: The left slope is −1 and the right slope +1, so no two-sided derivative exists. B: A zero function height does not determine the slope at a corner. C: A two-sided derivative cannot be chosen from only the left slope. D: The right-hand slope alone does not give the two-sided derivative.

questions.prompt: If g(x)=f(x)+7 on an interval and f is differentiable, how does the graph of g′ compare with the graph of f′?
options: It is shifted upward by 7.
They coincide.
It is shifted right by 7.
It is stretched vertically by a factor of 7.
questions.explanation: Differentiate g=f+7 to obtain g′=f′. Therefore their derivative graphs coincide at every interval input. Although the original graphs have different heights, their corresponding tangent slopes are identical. A: The constant shift vanishes when differentiating. B: A constant vertical translation of a function changes no local slopes. C: The original transformation changes output, not input. D: Adding a constant does not multiply slopes.

questions.prompt: Let g(x)=f(−x) for a differentiable function on the real numbers. Which rule correctly transforms the derivative graph?
options: g′(x)=f′(−x): reflect only across the vertical axis.
g′(x)=−f′(x): reflect only across the horizontal axis.
g′(x)=−f′(−x): reflect the graph of f′ across the vertical axis and then across the horizontal axis.
g′(x)=f′(x): leave it unchanged for every f.
questions.explanation: The chain rule gives g′(x)=f′(−x)(−1). On a derivative graph, the argument −x reflects inputs across the vertical axis, and the leading minus reflects outputs across the horizontal axis. Both operations are required. A: This omits the derivative of the inner input −x. B: This omits the changed input to the original derivative. C: The input reflection is accompanied by the chain factor −1. D: An arbitrary derivative need not have the symmetry needed for that equality.

questions.prompt: The graph below is f′. Which description of f near x=0 is correct?
options: f has a local maximum at 0.
f has a local minimum at 0.
f has a horizontal tangent at 0.
f is increasing through an inflection point at 0.
questions.explanation: The derivative is positive throughout, so f increases through 0. To the left f′ increases, giving concave-up f; to the right f′ decreases, giving concave-down f. Thus f has an inflection point at 0 with a nonzero slope, not a local extremum. A: The derivative remains positive on both sides, so the original function does not turn there. B: No negative-to-positive derivative crossing occurs. C: The derivative value there is 3, not zero. D: The derivative stays positive but changes from increasing to decreasing at its peak.

questions.prompt: Which description matches the derivative graph for f(x)=x³−3x?
options: An upward-opening parabola with zeros at −1 and 1 and vertex (0,−3).
A downward-opening parabola with zeros at −1 and 1.
An upward-opening parabola with vertex (0,0).
A straight line with slope 6.
questions.explanation: Differentiate termwise: f′=3x²−3. The positive leading coefficient makes an upward parabola; solving 3x²−3=0 gives ±1, and its vertex height at x=0 is −3. All three features must agree in the derivative sketch. A: The derivative is 3x²−3. B: The quadratic coefficient in the derivative is positive. C: This omits the constant −3 in the derivative. D: That describes a second-derivative trend, not the first derivative.

questions.prompt: Two differentiable functions have identical derivative graphs on the same connected interval. What can be concluded about their original graphs?
options: They must be exactly the same graph.
They differ by a constant vertical translation on that interval.
They must differ by a horizontal translation.
They can have unrelated shapes and different local slope patterns.
questions.explanation: If f′=g′ throughout the interval, then (f−g)′=0 there. The Mean Value Theorem implies f−g is a constant on the connected interval. Their original graphs therefore have the same shape and can differ only in height. A: The shared derivative does not determine the additive constant. B: Their difference has derivative zero everywhere, so the Mean Value Theorem makes it constant. C: Equal slopes at matching inputs do not imply a horizontal shift. D: Identical derivatives impose identical matching-input slopes.

questions.prompt: The graph below is f′. What is f(2)−f(0)?
questions.explanation: The displayed derivative is −2 everywhere between 0 and 2. Thus f is a line of slope −2 there up to an additive constant. Its change is f(2)−f(0)=(−2)(2−0)=−4. The absolute height is not needed. A: This is the slope, not the change over two input units. B: This loses the negative sign of the constant slope. C: The derivative is the constant −2 on [0,2], so the output change is slope times interval length. D: A constant derivative does not make the original function constant unless that derivative is zero.
